en: Volume Three, Part Two, composed by Li Tongxuan of the Great Tang at Beiping.
The Ten Dedications. The Ten Dedications.

The first is the spiritual friend who saves all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings and dedicates [the merit] toward enlightenment; this takes the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) as primary, with the other nine as its companions.
The meaning of "Namo" (South) is as before.

There is a land named Vast and Expansive; by means of this, one turns back the previous ten abodes and ten practices, extensively cultivating the mind of liberation for oneself, causing it to be identical with birth-and-death, thereby harmonizing birth-and-death and nirvana.
The fragrance of wisdom that transforms all sentient beings as the Bodhisattvas advance through the five stages causes them to fulfill the vast ocean of Samantabhadra’s great vows.
Taking this as the primary cause, the kingdom was named "Vast" (Guangda).

There was an elder who sold incense; because he was skilled at blending various fragrances, it symbolized his ability to harmonize and treat birth and death, thereby becoming the fragrance of great wisdom, great compassion, and the fivefold dharma-body of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
He universally perfumes all sentient beings, causing them all to resolve their minds [for enlightenment]; therefore, he is named "Selling Incense" (Yuxiang).
Selling Incense melts away and transforms mundane existence into supramundane liberation, entering into birth and death to achieve great wisdom and great compassion as a single, non-dual entity.

Liberation is indestructible and can become one with birth and death, just as pure water remains unclouded even when situated in mud; just as a crystal gem placed in turbid water can clarify that turbid water, yet the nature of the water remains clear even while it is present; just as stinking grass exists within a sandalwood grove; and just as wondrous lotuses grow from turbid water.

Furthermore, it is like the *āñjana* medicinal herb: one *liang* of it can transform a thousand *liang* of copper or iron into true gold, such that they become entirely of a golden substance, devoid of any nature of copper or iron.

If a person, for even a single thought-moment, accords with the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance, they can harmonize the evil karma of beginningless ignorance and transform it into the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and great compassion.

It is like various fragrances being blended together into a single pellet; they mutually perfume one another to produce a sublime flavor, yet the essences of the various fragrances do not know one another. Whether pure or mixed, they function with total freedom; each individual fragrance neither joins nor separates from the others.

Therefore, by means of pure wisdom, the Bodhisattva regards birth and death as one with himself; the eighty-four thousand unspeakable gateways of affliction of all sentient beings are all, together with him, perfected as an ocean of wisdom and compassion.
Birth-and-death is without defilement, and wisdom is without purity; there is no blending and no combining, neither dispersal nor separation.
If one perceives birth-and-death as turbid and perceives wisdom as pure, one then dwells within the two minds of defilement and purity.
The state of mind is nothing other than liberation.
This is because the elder named Blue Lotus (Utpala) illustrates how one dwells within birth and death without being defiled.

In these ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), one turns back the supramundane minds of the preceding ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*) to enter into birth and death and thereby accomplish great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Because they are free from defilement and attachment, they are represented by the blue lotus of the lay elder.
At the beginning of the ten stages (bhūmi) and the beginning of the ten practices (caryā), monks are placed first in both cases to represent the predominance of the supramundane mind.
Having already attained transcendence of the world, one must enter the cycle of birth and death to extensively traverse the ocean of practice in order to deliver sentient beings.
For this reason, these ten dedications are symbolized by the title "Blue Lotus," using the name of a worldly elder as a metaphorical representation.
Consider this deeply: by returning to the mundane from the ultimate and engaging with the various defilements (*kleśa*), one remains untainted by those defilements.

When the Elder says, "I know all fragrances," he clarifies that all sentient beings possess the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*); it is simply that the time for their aspiration to arise has not yet arrived.
All incense represents those who, within the ocean of birth and death, teach and transform others to bring about awakening by burning away afflictions.
All unguents represent those who, with clarity, console and praise all sentient beings within the ocean of birth and death, causing them to rejoice and resolve their minds toward enlightenment.
"All powdered incense" refers to causing all sentient beings to scatter their afflictions.

"Also knowing the source of the king of incense" means that the king of incense of fundamental wisdom emerges from within ignorance; by penetrating ignorance, it becomes fundamental wisdom as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Being sovereign as a king, it cannot be defiled by the myriad objects of the senses.

Below this, the eight classes of beings, such as the Deva-gandharvas and Nāga-gandharvas, possess eight kinds of incense; this clarifies how the eight kinds of wrong reflection among the eight classes of worldly humans, devas, and other beings are transformed into the eightfold right path within the Noble Way through harmonious integration.

Below, there are thirteen kinds of incense—comprising both excellent and foul fragrances as well as those enjoyed by the world—which clarify the six sense organs within the six realms of humans and devas, along with the twelve [types of] wholesome, unwholesome, and afflictive states regarding their objects; these are combined into a single pellet to form the incense of the "saintly knowledge, vision, and enjoyment," which thus totals thirteen.
The following describes the distinct fragrances of the bodhisattvas, which represent their distinct wisdoms.
The "fragrance of all bodhisattva stages" clarifies the progressive advancement through the distinctions of the five positions.
To summarize the forms, origins, and fundamental natures of such fragrances as these is to clarify the characteristics of the arising of advancement through the five stages of integration.

For instance, within the Ten Abodes, there are ten stages of arising; in each case, the subsequent stage precedes the preceding one, leading the practitioner to advance without stagnation, ensuring that their preparatory application (*prayoga*) does not cease, and causing wisdom, virtue, compassion, and all arts to be swiftly clarified, while the path of practice expands and broadens so as not to be hindered by any single dharma.
Furthermore, from the first stage of generating the mind of enlightenment up to the third stage, the supramundane mind manifests.

This is illustrated by taking the householder Megha of the marketplace as the point of departure; this is done because the supramundane mind of the preceding stages is predominant therein, thereby causing one to realize that even amidst the clamor of the marketplace, there is the supramundane.

From the fourth dwelling to the sixth dwelling, there is a predominance of both mundane and supramundane minds; however, in the seventh dwelling, one enters purely into the cycle of birth and death without seeking the supramundane, taking the practice of great compassion as the means of arising, each of which consists of ten stages.

Furthermore, regarding the two instances of arising—the fourth and the seventh—the subsequent ten dwellings take the ten practices as their arising; the ten practices take the ten dedications as their arising; and this applies to all five stages in the same manner.
If it were not thus, one might obtain a single dharma and immediately claim it is sufficient, thereby ceasing all further seeking.

In the human realm there is a fragrance called "Elephant-Treasury" (*hastigarbha*), which arises from the battle of dragons; this clarifies that the elephant represents great power, containing within its body a vast function. It symbolizes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) being obscured by ignorance and craving; only when one uses the power of meditative concentration and wisdom to observe and confront the dragons of greed, anger, and attachment does one finally manifest this fragrance.

If one burns a single pellet such that it raises a great cloud of incense pervading the royal capital, its measure would encompass all of empty space; for the realm of birth and death is the royal capital, as the wise dwell therein.

For seven days, a fine rain of subtle fragrance fell; those upon whom it settled all became golden in color. Through the struggle between illumination and ignorance, he manifested the fundamental wisdom, pure and stainless; then, by giving rise to the wisdom of differentiation, he preached the sublime Dharma of the seven treasures of purity.
If one is able to awaken and enter [this state], such that body and mind are pure and stainless, it is called "golden.

If even the clothing, palaces, and pavilions one wears or inhabits are all golden, this clarifies the various practices conducive to the Path—namely, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
They are all entirely golden in color, which clarifies that the myriad practices take fundamental wisdom as their essence.

As for the wind blowing them into the golden palace, this clarifies that through the wind of the spoken teachings, they enter the minds of sentient beings, who then believe and accept the contemplation of the seven factors of enlightenment.
That which is described as being filled with joy for seven days and seven nights refers to the bliss of the Dharma (*dharmasukha*), as explained extensively in the sutras.

Together with this "Elephant-Treasury Incense" (*hastigarbha-gandha*) listed below, there are ten types of incense in total. These five categories are used universally; for instance, in the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), one type of incense is assigned to each abode. Likewise, for the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), the Ten Transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*), and the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), each of these ten stages is likewise assigned its own specific type of incense.
The fifth is like the fragrance from within the Snowy Mountains, representing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The sixth is the fragrance from within the realm of the *rākṣasas*, representing the sixth [perfection], wisdom (*prajñā*).
Wisdom is likened to a *rākṣasa* because it can devour the flesh and blood of sentient beings, and its power and function are fierce and robust.
The dharmas of the corresponding stage that are symbolized clarify that the wisdom-rākṣasa destroys ignorance; it cannot be countered.
The fragrance of this rākṣasa-realm is named "Ocean-Treasury," for it takes wisdom as its ocean-treasury.

The fact that this incense is used exclusively by a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) clarifies that once the sixth stage—the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—has been perfected, one is then able to skillfully turn the wheel of the Dharma, resembling a wheel-turning monarch.

When a single pellet is burned and the fourfold army all ascends into the void, it clarifies that upon reaching the stage of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Dharma taught, as well as body, mind, and the four analytical eloquences (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*), all merge with emptiness; though each is grasped as an image, once the Dharma-image is attained, it vanishes.
From the passage "I have only known this method of harmonizing various fragrances" onwards, there is an exaltation of virtue and advancement.

This clarifies that while the preceding ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*) involved much effort in generating a mind that transcends birth and death, this stage of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) enables one to enter into the cycle of birth and death without attachment, thereby giving rise to the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
Furthermore, because it constitutes the essence of great wisdom and great compassion for the subsequent ten stages as well as the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*),
and because it was taught while residing in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace within the realm of the desire world (*kāmadhātu*).

By means of this harmonization of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) with the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, one fully completes the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), because one acts according to the model.

In the preceding sutra, light was emitted from the knees to explain the ten stages of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); the knee symbolizes the meaning of mastery over contraction and expansion, manifesting that at this stage one attains mastery by harmonizing saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; therefore, the method of blending incense is employed here as its symbolic representation.

The second is the non-deteriorating dedication (*avipraṇāśa-pariṇāmanā*), which takes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) as its primary element and the other nine perfections as its companions.

It takes the wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*) of the indestructible, pure *dharmakāya* as the essence of ethical discipline. Taking this pure essence of ethical discipline as great compassion, one dwells within the birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) of the world while realizing that the nature of birth-and-death is entirely pure.
If one dwells in delusion, both mind and objects are bound;
if one dwells in awakening, both mind and objects are true.
Therefore, it is called the "unbreakable dedication."
In this southern direction—the meaning of "south" being as previously explained—there is a great city named Lokeśvara-alaṃkāra (Adorned with Palaces).
It is so named because its palaces are formed by the observation of the various faculties (*indriya*) through immeasurable, multilayered, and diverse forms of wisdom.
In this inexhaustible ocean of wisdom, he receives and guides sentient beings according to their faculties and the times, serving as a pavilion.
There is a captain named Vasiṣṭha, which translates here as "Sovereign.
He is called "Sovereign" because, in this station, he dwells within the cycle of birth and death through pure precepts without being defiled by it.

The shipmaster who stands outside the city gate does so for the sake of receiving sentient beings; because he does not abide in his own wisdom and virtue, he remains on the outside to receive sentient beings.

Regarding "upon the seashore," this stage takes great compassion as its essential nature (śīla); it clarifies that one stands upon the shore of birth and death to receive sentient beings, ensuring there is no loss of the proper time, just as the tide of the great ocean never misses its appointed hour.
The fact that he was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of merchants and other immeasurable multitudes clarifies the perfection of his myriad practices.
The ship’s captain said:
“In this city, along the coastal road, I have purely cultivated the practice of the Bodhisattva’s banner of great compassion.”

This is because those who clearly understand the path of wandering within the great ocean of birth and death, and who purely cultivate the practice of the Bodhisattva’s banner of great compassion, are unshakable while remaining within birth and death, and because they utterly destroy all the armies of birth and death.
This shipmaster has two meanings:

first, because the Bodhisattva constantly dwells in the world to rescue those in distress, manifesting conduct identical to that of ordinary beings, he acts as a great shipmaster who leads all sentient beings, the merchants, to the place of jewels; he distinguishes the various kinds of jewels and determines their value—tasks that cannot be accomplished except through noble wisdom.

Second is the demonstration of the Dharma: it clarifies that in this stage, great compassion constitutes the essence of the precepts. While the ten abodes and ten practices enable one to emerge from the ocean of birth and death, this stage involves turning back to enter the ocean of birth and death in order to rescue and ferry across sentient beings submerged within it; therefore, it is likened to the image of a boatman.
Therefore, the boatman said:
"Those who hear my Dharma shall not fear the ocean of birth and death, and will surely enter the ocean of all-knowledge.
This is explained at length as set forth in the sutra.
From the section "Having received from me only this Dharma-gate of the Practice of the Banner of Great Compassion" onwards, this constitutes the advancement through the attribution of merit.
The third is the dedication equal to all Buddhas, which takes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its primary element, with the other nine perfections as its companions.
The meaning of "South" (Nan) is as explained previously.
There is a city named "Delightful" (Kelo). This city signifies the advancement from the preceding stage to this present stage.

"City" (Cheng) carries the sense of protection; it is so named because within the state of mind and its objects, anger and resentment never arise, and there is no heart of jealousy—thus it is called a city.
The city is called "Delightful" because those who constantly practice patience are a joy for all to behold.
The elder is named "Unsurpassed Victor," which clarifies that among all practices, patience is the most supreme.
The reason Sudhana weeps and sheds tears at this stage is to clarify the practice of patience and compassion.
Seeing the merchant leader Anupamavijaya to the east of the city signifies that he is the foremost in bringing forth and illuminating the manifold virtues born of springtime.

Regarding the "Great Adornment Forest, Banner of the Forest of No-Sorrow": it is the dwelling place where one achieves fulfillment through the mind of patience and remains free from sorrow amidst the myriad practices.
Regarding the "residing of immeasurable merchants": it refers to seeking the treasure of the Dharma.
The "hundreds of thousands of lay devotees" refers to those who abide in the mundane world yet remain eternally true.
That he is "surrounded by the various assemblies as described above" signifies that his engagement with sentient beings and his practice have reached perfection.

Sudhana saw the elder and threw himself upon the ground, prostrating at his feet; after a long while he rose, having paid homage with the profound wisdom accomplished through the practice of clear patience.
The Elder Anuttaravara said:
"I have accomplished the gate of the Bodhisattva practice that reaches all places, a supernormal power that is independent and unconditioned.

First he spoke of all among the people within the trichiliocosm; next, he spoke of the Heaven of the Thirty-three and the eight classes of nāgas and spirits, extending even to the bodies in all lands and the evil realms of hell throughout the ten directions, pervading them all. By teaching through the use of their own kind, he caused them all to rejoice; according to what each vessel could bear, he caused them all to be free from suffering.

Through the realization of the dharma-patience, it is immediately accomplished, and non-reliant wisdom manifests. Because this wisdom has no location—neither large, small, middle, nor boundary—it is not subsumed within the three periods of time; its nature is inherently all-pervasive, its measure encompassing the entire dharma-realm, reaching without going and arriving without coming.
This is the divine within the non-divine, its great function pervading everywhere;
the unconditioned within the conditioned, its great efficacy universally responding.

Throughout the ten directions and the six realms, it constantly manifests a physical body before all sentient beings, teaching and transforming them according to their needs. It appears as an ordinary being among all things, yet no sentient beings harbor doubts or feelings of strangeness.
This is the constant state of the worlds of humans and devas throughout the ten directions; it is the eternal path of Samantabhadra.
This serves as a model, enabling practitioners who have not yet reached their goal to recognize their station and joyfully strive to attain it; thus, this [teaching] is not without its purpose.

"I only know this Dharma-gate of purifying the bodhisattva practice that reaches all places, which possesses the power of spiritual penetrations that are non-reliant and non-active. From here on, this is the section on recommending virtues and advancing upward.

The three figures preceding these represent the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), wherein one enters the cycle of birth and death to accomplish the practice of great compassion; they are symbolized by the three lay elders: the incense merchant named Blue Lotus (*Utpala*), the boatman Īśvara, and the elder Anuttarajaya.

Proceeding further south, there is a land called Śūna, where there is a bhikṣuṇī named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā. Because she has entered into the mundane and supramundane compassion within the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*), she is represented here by a bhikṣuṇī.
The character "Ni" (尼) is the sound of compassion.
A "Bhikṣu" (比丘) is the mark of transcending the world; it signifies the practice of great compassion that is pure and emerges from within the cycle of birth and death.

This is to clarify that while practitioners realize the nature of birth and death is pure, they take pity on those who do not understand, as such people remain perpetually within it with no prospect of escape.
The fourth dedication, "Dedication Reaching All Places," clarifies this practice of vigor, for there is no place of birth and death it does not pervade and no evil realm it does not reach.
With the perfection of diligence as the primary factor, the other nine serve as its companions.
The meaning of "South" is as explained previously.
There is a land named Sūna, which here is translated as "Valiant."

For this reason, while situated within the cycle of birth and death, he practices great compassion and delivers beings; his measure is equal to the realm of empty space, manifesting forms according to the capacities of sentient beings throughout the six realms, pervading everywhere so that there is none who is not saved.
Because his diligence was such as this, the land was named "Valiant.

In that land there was a city named Kalingavana, which in this language means "Time of Strife. It was so named because it clarifies that this stage remains unstained by the world, and that through great compassion one can harmonize strife within the world.

The bhikṣuṇī named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā was so named because her virtuous conduct established her reputation; she possessed clear and pure wisdom like that of a lion. Having long dwelt within saṃsāra, out of great compassion she extensively delivered sentient beings without shrinking from toil or weariness, her mind always remaining joyful and at ease; thus she was called Vijṛmbhitā.
"Stretching like a lion" (*siṃha-vijṛmbhita*) signifies the sense of unfolding, relaxing, and finding joy.

This bhikṣuṇī resides within the garden donated by King Prasenajit; because she has attained mastery by practicing the great compassionate conduct that transcends birth and death amidst the cycle of saṃsāra, she is thus named after King Prasenajit.

This garden of relinquishment and giving is so named because it clarifies the practice of the Dharma of loving-kindness and compassion; because it demonstrates that one dwelling within birth and death is superior to birth and death; and because it takes the practice of compassionate giving as its source of joy. Thus, it is called a "garden."

"Udyāna" (Garden) signifies the meaning of wandering, viewing, and finding joy; it is named a garden because it symbolizes how a Bodhisattva constantly dwells within birth and death, taking the liberation of sentient beings as their own pleasure.

In this stage, through the wisdom of universal radiance, one accomplishes various types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) to benefit the ten directions; manifesting a single body as infinite bodies, one appears before all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*, thereby accomplishing the gates of differentiated wisdom.

This clarifies that this practice of the vigor of compassion and loving-kindness encompasses all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions of space as a single whole; through great compassion, it benefits these beings, causing them to leave suffering behind and attain happiness, to resolve upon the bodhicitta, and to achieve the unsurpassed path.
In this vast garden, not a single sentient being is exhausted or excluded.
All the bodhisattvas therein act in this same manner, because the fundamental nature of the realm of sentient beings is such; thus, she is likened to the bhikṣuṇī named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā.
All the jewel trees, ponds, pavilions, and so forth within the garden are adorned with the retribution of practicing clear reliance, as explained at length in the sutra.
From the passage beginning "I only know this much of the accomplishment of all-knowledge" onwards, this is the section on advancing by extolling virtues.
The fifth is the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit, which takes the dhyāna-pāramitā as its primary element and the other nine as its companions.
To the south lies a land called Durga (The Perilous), so named because it practices the arts of women and thereby violates the True Principle; thus, those who hear of it find it difficult to believe.

As for the city named Ratnavyūha, because he attained great compassion upon reaching its location, he constantly followed the stream of birth and death to extensively benefit all classes of beings, practicing together with them to bring benefit to living beings.
Having realized that the nature of the five desires is non-existent, one does not depart from the essence of dhyāna.
Because of great compassion, one does not depart from the essence of the mundane world.
For the sake of great wisdom, one dwells in the mundane world without being defiled.
Now, to fear and distance oneself from the realms of the mundane world is the Dharma of the Two Vehicles;
to become defiled by and attached to them is the Dharma of ordinary beings.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva does not conform to either of these two: out of great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), he dwells within birth and death to practice in common with others; and out of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
He has realized that both birth-and-death and the realms of the world are entirely non-existent.
Out of great compassion, he manifests his body through the illusion of wisdom; he dwells in the world like a shadow, just like a conjured person.
Although they dwell within the world, there is no object that can defile them, nor is there a mind that defiles objects.
Yet, for the sake of the practice of great compassion, they do not engage in even a single worldly action, but rather practice the infinite gateways of conduct appropriate to all sentient beings.
Although one is in the world, the world is like a transformation and one’s own body is like an illusion; thus, one follows sensory objects with wisdom.
Since there is no one who is defiled by these objects, the objects themselves are fundamentally non-existent.
For this reason, although he conforms to worldly conventions, he remains eternally detached from the realm of desire.

Through this Dharma-gate, he clarifies that his own wisdom is free from the five desires; yet, out of great compassion, he constantly enters the cycle of birth and death to benefit sentient beings in accordance with worldly customs, thereby attaining great merit.
The fifth is named the Dedication of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit; thus, the city is named Jewel Adornment (*Ratnavyūha*).
Because he possesses no five desires through his own wisdom and practices the ten thousand deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, the city is named Jewel Adornment.

Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "He manifests the experience of the five desires and also displays the practice of dhyāna, causing the mind of Māra to become confused and agitated, so that he cannot find an opportunity."
"A lotus blooming amidst fire is truly a marvel;
practicing dhyāna while remaining in the realm of desire is likewise a marvel.
In this stage, great compassion constitutes the essence of dhyāna; dwelling in the world without being defiled, as exemplified by the woman Vāsukī.
This represents the practice of the great compassion of all bodhisattvas; since the dharmas are identical within the entanglements, it is not necessarily required that she be a woman.
For if one were to depart from worldly conduct, there would likewise be no bodhisattva practice.
Because sentient beings have many afflictions, the practices of a bodhisattva are many;
because sentient beings lack afflictions, the practices of a bodhisattva likewise do not exist.
The aforementioned bhikṣuṇī, by entering into the cycle of birth and death, has perfected great compassion and attained the gate of compassionate practice that issues from supramundane liberation.

In this stage, while abiding in supramundane liberation and compassion, she enters the realms of the five desires; because she clarifies the great benevolence of the Bodhisattva mind, she is unstained while stained and stained while unstained. She manifests the experience of the five desires yet does not fail in her feminine resolve, nor does she damage the dhyāna-gate of the unconditioned self-nature. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, according to those who behold her, she appears in various distinct bodies as appropriate to each.

When Sudhana saw the woman Vasumitrā—here translated as "World-Friend" (Shiyou)—because she was able to manifest her physical form in all worlds throughout the ten directions, appearing as a friend to each according to their faculties and never abandoning them, causing all to leave suffering and attain happiness, she was thus called "World-Friend."

Regarding the statement that "he dwells in his own home to the north of the marketplace": he takes this state of birth-and-death and worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) as the marketplace, and the non-existence of any phenomenon that is not quiescent as his own home.

That his dwelling is vast and magnificent, with walls, trees, gardens, and pavilions all adorned with jewels, arises from the fruit of retribution attained through the pervasive presence of the essence of dhyāna and the perfection of the myriad practices.

If there are those who hear the Dharma and obtain the opportunity to see and draw near to it, there are none who do not gain benefit; they depart from the limit of greed and desire, as explained at length in the sutras.

As for dwelling in a house situated to the north of the marketplace, this symbolizes that the north corresponds to the Black Tortoise (Wuxu), which presides over villainy, thieves, and bandits, and is the realm of the darkness of night.

Because Bodhisattvas constantly dwell within the marketplace of birth and death—the long night of ignorance—they engage with the stream of deluded beings to lead them back to right view; thus, they employ the skillful means of desire to transform those who are lost.
Sudhana asked, "What meritorious deeds did you cultivate to attain such sovereign mastery?

The girl replied, "In the past, there was a Buddha named 'High Conduct' (Gocara). Because the essence of this dhyāna-position was lofty and supreme, transcending all conceptual thoughts and views, the Buddha was given the name 'High Conduct.'"
As for the city named "Wondrous Gate" (Sudvāra), it is called "Wondrous Gate" because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*).

When that Buddha entered the royal city and stepped upon its threshold, the entire city shook; this illustrates that when concentration and wisdom are in accord, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are utterly destroyed.

As for that city suddenly becoming vast and expansive, adorned with various jewels: because it accords with the essence of dhyāna, the mind has no interior or exterior and its measure is equal to empty space; thus it is called "vast and expansive."

Without impairing the essence of meditative concentration, one enters into *samānārthatā* (acting in common) to receive sentient beings; thus, one attains the adornments of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, for one never departs from the mastery of *dhyāna-samādhi*.
I, who am the wife of the elder, take meditative concentration as my husband and the mind of compassion as my wife.
By means of clarity, I do not lose the state of meditative concentration; through great compassion, I follow worldly customs without being defiled.

Regarding the offering of a single precious coin to that Buddha: among things circulating in the world, nothing is more precious than a precious coin; likewise, among those circulating in the world as the Noble Path, nothing surpasses wisdom.
Mañjuśrī serves as the Buddha’s attendant; he is the wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*) of fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*).

Taking this fundamental gnosis as the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and manifesting wondrous wisdom as his attendant, he teaches and transforms sentient beings to inspire them toward bodhicitta. Because this is the sovereign power of a Bodhisattva, he clarifies that while the mind of dhyāna remains indestructible, he is nonetheless able to conform to worldly conventions. This demonstrates that the great wisdom and great compassion of a Bodhisattva constitute the essence of dhyāna; even while dwelling in the marketplace of birth and death, neither defilement nor purity can obstruct his dhyāna, and neither clamor nor contention can detain his nature.
From the passage "Since I have known only this liberation door of the limit of freedom from desire" onwards, this is the advancement through the attribution of virtues.
The sixth is the dedication of firm conformity, which takes the *prajñāpāramitā* as its primary element and the other nine perfections as its companions.
The meaning of "South" (Nan) is as explained previously.

There is a city named Śubhavatī; because it is perfected through the wisdom and compassion of this sixth stage of the Prajñāpāramitā, and because it skillfully delivers all classes of beings, the city is named Śubhavatī.

There was a householder named Viśvantara, which here is translated as "Inclusive" (Bāoshè), signifying that the wisdom of this stage is boundless, encompassing all myriad virtues and rescuing and gathering in all sentient beings.
He constantly made offerings at the stūpa of the Candanāsana Buddha; this was to clarify that sandalwood is a fragrant tree capable of neutralizing the fiery venom of snakes.
By means of this, the lay devotee always sits upon the fragrant seat of wisdom and liberation, able to eliminate the feverish afflictions of all sentient beings.
A stūpa is the dwelling place of the Buddha’s physical form.
This particular stūpa contains only a sandalwood throne, and no image is placed upon it; this is to clarify that he sits upon the throne of emptiness-wisdom (*śūnyatā-prajñā*).
To regard it as a Buddha-stūpa is to clarify that the wisdom of emptiness is the gate of liberation wherein the Buddha is imperishable.
Upon opening the sandalwood throne-stūpa, one immediately attains samādhi.
As for the name "Inexhaustible Seed of the Buddha," it clarifies that when the wisdom of unconditioned emptiness manifests before one, this is the inexhaustibility of the Buddha-seed.

It is also the universal vision of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and it is the gate of the non-extinction of the Buddhas; for by means of this dharma of unconditioned, empty wisdom, there is neither arising nor ceasing, it is eternally functional yet perpetually quiescent, and it is shared equally by all Buddhas.
Because it can destroy birth and death and its spiritual function is sovereign;
like an echo in space, it responds in accordance with conditions, universally responding throughout the ten directions, without going or coming.

Therefore, when a lay practitioner makes offerings to a *candana* throne Buddha-stūpa, they attain the Dharma-gate of the Buddha’s non-extinction. Taking the wisdom of emptiness as the substance of the throne, they come to perceive that within the *candana* throne Buddha-stūpa there is no physical form or image; this is precisely because the Buddha does not undergo extinction.
Because the wisdom of luminous emptiness is itself the Buddha, there is no such thing as extinction (nirvāṇa).
They merely came to visit the stupa, attained the Way, and departed; therefore, the city is named Śrāvastī (Good Crossing).
From the passage "Having received from me this Bodhisattva liberation-gate of the limit of non-nirvāṇa" onwards, this is the advancement through the cultivation of virtues.

Regarding the seventh dedication, "dedicating equally toward all sentient beings," it clarifies that among the five stages, the seventh all employs the sixth dharma-gate of the wisdom of emptiness to accord with all sentient beings; dwelling within birth and death, one accomplishes the practice of great compassion, and thus it is called "the dedication that accords with all sentient beings."
With the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) as the primary element, the other nine serve as its companions.
The meaning of the southern direction is as explained previously.
There is a mountain named Potalaka, which in this language is translated as "Mountain of Small White Flower Trees"; on that mountain, there are many small white flower trees.

This represents Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva abiding in the practice of great compassion to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them not to commit even minor wrongs and not to abandon even minor virtues, but to carry out every single good deed, however minute.

Since the great arises from the small, and as thin frost accumulates until hard ice arrives, or fine dust gathers until mountains and peaks are formed, the sage therefore warns against minor transgressions as if they were major offenses, and practices minor virtues so that great goodness may spontaneously be achieved.
However, since the nature of all dharmas is inherently empty and void, not even a subtle thought can arise; thus, [the cycle of] right and wrong is exhausted.
For this reason, Avalokiteśvara dwells upon Mount Pāṇḍukambala, manifesting through acts of compassion.
The rendering of "Guānzìzài" (Avalokiteśvara) in the old sutra is incorrect;
following the new sutra as "Guānshìyīn" (Avalokitasvara) is correct, as it expresses the meaning of great compassion.

To the west of this mountain, within the rocky valleys, Sudhana saw Avalokiteśvara seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon a diamond-jewel stone, with immeasurable bodhisattvas all likewise seated on jewel stones to the west of the mountain.

Regarding the one seated upon a diamond-jewel throne within the mountain ravines: the western face of the mountain and the ravines represent that the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion constantly dwells amidst all perilous and evil paths to practice the conduct of great compassion; thus, the mountain and the western ravines together signify the various evil realms where he practices the conduct of great compassion.
This is because the West is clarified as being the White Tiger, as metal, as the autumnal season of killing, and as malevolent harm.

To manifest great compassion through the practice of compassion within the evil destinies, there is [the presence of] the Vajra-Jewel Throne in every direction of the East and in every direction of the West; it is thus throughout the ten directions.

Regarding the non-manifestation of various wondrous palaces, towers, and adornments: this clarifies that through firm and steadfast great compassion, he does not abandon any sentient beings in the evil destinies; because he constantly manifests various bodily forms within the evil realms to deliver sentient beings, remaining without retreat or wavering, he sits upon the diamond-jewel throne.

The same was true for the precious stones upon which the other bodhisattvas sat; because they constantly concealed their forms within the evil realms to benefit sentient beings of their own kind, they did not manifest the splendor of their own karmic rewards.

He constantly preached the Sūtra of Compassion for the great assembly; for Sudhana, he expounded the gate of liberation consisting of the practice of great compassion, because in all places he always gathered in sentient beings through kind words, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
From the passage "Having received from me only this Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Great Compassion" onwards, there is the advancement through the attribution of virtues.

This is the eighth dedication, the Aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*), which clarifies that in this stage the wisdom-stage increases in clarity, such that both the mental object and the subjective mind are truly real.
By dedicating through this true wisdom, one enters the cycle of birth and death while abiding in the true essence.
Here, the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) is primary, with the other nine as its companions.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the eastern direction named Samantagāmin (Correctly Proceeding). Since all the preceding stages were described as being in the southern direction, why is it that this stage alone is said to be in the east?
By means of these ten dedications, one returns to the ultimate truth while entering the conventional world, thereby accomplishing the practice of great compassion.
These seventh and eighth stages are the synthesis of the essence of compassion and wisdom.
The east symbolizes wisdom, as it is the vanguard that brings forth manifestation through the springtime of birth.
The west symbolizes compassion (*karuṇā*), for it represents the autumn that brings about the hidden end of the bright cycle.
To symbolize the correct path, this is wisdom (*prajñā*); Avalokiteśvara is compassion. Wisdom and compassion are harmoniously united, being non-dual in essence.
He pointed out his place of origin, saying that he had come here from the presence of the Buddha Universal Victorious Birth in the world-system Wondrous Treasury in the eastern direction.

Furthermore, regarding the duration of time since he departed from that Buddha’s realm, he said it had been an incalculable number of kalpas, as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field. In every single thought-moment, he took steps as numerous as the atoms within an incalculable number of buddha-fields, traversing buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms within an incalculable times incalculable number of worlds. In each and every buddha-field, he entered everywhere to reach the presence of those Buddhas, making offerings with all manner of ritual implements.

These various offerings are produced by the unsurpassed mind and sealed by non-conceptual wisdom; they extend even to the teaching and transformation of all sentient beings in the lower realms, as extensively described in the sutras.

Furthermore, when Sudhana sees the Bodhisattva Samantagamin, he sees him in the same assembly as Avalokiteśvara; this clarifies that the wisdom and compassion of Avalokiteśvara and Samantagamin are of one essence.

Furthermore, it is indicated that the seventh stage is the increase of compassion (*karuṇā*) and the eighth stage is the increase of wisdom (*jñāna*); this clarifies that by attaining the increase of the essence of wisdom through the correct course, one returns to the station of compassion—this is seen from the perspective of the assembly of Avalokiteśvara.

He came from the presence of the Buddha Universal Victorious Birth in the world called Wondrous Treasury in the eastern direction. He takes the sublime wisdom of the Dharma-body—which is bodiless and signless—as his world; it is an ocean of non-active wisdom of universal radiance, pure by its very nature, whose essence spontaneously pervades the lands and realms of the ten directions, and he is named the Buddha Universal Victorious Birth.

From this fundamental wisdom of universal radiance, the wisdom of differentiation arises; in a single thought-moment, it pervades before all Buddhas and all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, manifesting bodies according to their needs to make offerings to the Buddhas and to teach and transform sentient beings, appearing universally in the ten directions simultaneously without coming or going.
The Master of the Treatise states in verse: "Just as the sun and moon appear everywhere within rivers, oceans, ponds, pools, and all flowing springs, manifesting without exception;
yet their forms neither come nor go, and their reflections and light pervade all places. The nature of these reflections and their original substances is like space."
The karmic power of sentient beings arises, yet the nature of karma has no coming or going; fundamental wisdom is likewise, its essence and characteristics like empty space.

Its radiance illuminates the ten directions, universally appearing in the waters of sentient beings; it teaches and transforms the multitudes of the ten directions and makes offerings to all Buddhas, yet there is no agent capable of doing so, for wisdom is sovereign.
"The Spirit's function fills the ten directions, yet within the Spirit there is no Spirit; such is the power of the Spirit.

Thus, this great function and spiritual power pervade everywhere, as do the various implements of offering. The Sūtra says: "All these are accomplished by the unsurpassed mind and sealed by the unconditioned Dharma."
This is because the essence of the wisdom of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) is adorned with immeasurable merits and karmic virtues.

In brief, once this Avalokiteśvara has entered the gate of the non-duality of wisdom and compassion through the "Correct Entrance" (*samyak-praveśa*), he remains within the gate of compassion from the seventh dedication until reaching the tenth dedication of immeasurable merit.
Because Avalokiteśvara is the embodiment of all great compassion throughout all times and ages, and because his wisdom and compassion are vast, he does not depart from his fundamental nature.
Even the manifestations up to the tenth bhūmi do not depart from Avalokiteśvara; all Buddhas likewise do not depart from him.
This first establishes the model, which subsequent positions then emulate.
From "Having attained this bodhisattva liberation door of universal and swift movement" onwards, it is the advancement through the promotion of virtues.
The ninth is the dedication of liberation free from bondage and attachment, which takes the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) as its primary element, with the other nine as its companions.
To the south there is a city named Dvāravatī, which in this language means "Possessing Gates."
Because this station is the ninth station of the Dharma Master and possesses a great Dharma-gate, the city is named "Possessing Gates" (Sadvatī).
Within it dwells a celestial deity named Mahādeva; having seen him, Sudhana prostrated himself in reverence and made his request.

Mahādeva extended his four hands, took up the waters of the four great oceans to wash his own face, and held various golden flowers to scatter over Sudhana, thereby illustrating the reverence shown toward those who have first resolved their minds on enlightenment.
Furthermore, he extended his four hands, encompassing all with the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
He washed his own face and, with the eye of pure wisdom, observed sentient beings to discern their faculties and guide them accordingly.
For the sake of Sudhana, he expounded the Dharma-gate of the Cloud-Net.

"Heaven" (deva) carries the meanings of purity, compassion, and providing shelter; it signifies the universal containment and nurturing of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, clarifying that its protective covering is like a cloud that universally bestows moisture.
The teaching is established like a net for the purpose of filtering and gathering sentient beings.
For this reason, celestial deities bring forth treasures as vast as mountains to bestow upon those in need.
Through the contemplations of the five methods of cessation and stabilization (*pañca-nīvaraṇa-pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), they receive the Dharma according to their respective capacities.
This clarifies that the practitioner’s wisdom accords with the natural state and employs the wondrous Way; thus they transcend emotional fabrications and act through the exercise of wisdom.
Because they encompass all and bestow widely, they employ their faculties by relying on the true nature.

Taking the Great Deity (Mahādeva) as one's supreme friend clarifies the unconditioned essence of fundamental wisdom; this deity is so named because all dharma-gates emerge from it, and thus the city is called "The Gate of Existence."
From the passage "Since I have known only this Dharma-gate of the Cloud-Net" onwards, this is the advancement through the exaltation of virtues.
The tenth, the Dedication Equal to the Dharma-realm, takes the perfection of wisdom as its primary element, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.

Regarding the fact that there are kingdoms within this Jambudvīpa: because the dharma of dedication through the light that is equal to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is all-pervasive, it is collectively referred to as Jambudvīpa.
As for "in the Bodhimaṇḍa of the kingdom of Magadha," this signifies that this practice reaches the fundamental essence of bodhi.

There is an earth goddess named Anvaya (Abiding); the preceding celestial deity represents the wisdom of fundamental purity, while the earth goddess named Anvaya represents the essence of compassion within that wisdom.

The celestial deities bring forth treasures from within the heavens, and the earth deities bring forth treasures from within the earth; this clarifies the merit inherent in compassion and arises from the blessings felt by sentient beings.

The celestial deity is the sublime function of wisdom; the terrestrial deity is the eternal stillness of the compassion of wisdom. Because its function is eternally still, it is named "Abiding Unmoving"; the name is established because the heavens move while the earth is still.
These two types of practitioners of luminosity cultivate within the cycle of birth and death until they reach the fundamental source of quiescence and function;
even up to the fruit of the tenth stage, they never depart from these two dharmas.

In accordance with the subsequent model, one should ensure that within the stages of the ten bhūmis and the level of Equal Enlightenment, the habitual cultivation of compassion and wisdom reaches fulfillment without shifting; these two dharmas constitute a single dharma.

With heaven as the cover and earth as the support, the way of nurturing does not go beyond this Dharma of perfected wisdom and compassion; therefore, the images of heaven and earth are taken to represent the methods of wisdom, benevolence, covering, supporting, and nurturing.
Thus, heaven and earth provide nourishment through the transformative generation of the karma created by sentient beings;
the Great Way provides nourishment through the wondrous spirituality of wisdom and compassion.
Heaven and earth are impartial and thus all things are perfected; the Great Way is impartial and thus all deities are saved.
Without acting, they achieve; yet they accomplish the great works of the ten directions.
Without performing, they act; yet they perform throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Therefore, when the Earth-Ruling Goddess dwelt in peace, she pressed the earth with her toe, and hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* jewels spontaneously welled up.
He said to Sudhana:
"This treasure store now follows you; it is sustained by the power of the merit and the fruit of the roots of goodness you cultivated in the past."
This clarifies that his spirit is as tranquil as the earth; thus, the earth produces various treasures to adorn itself, for when the spirit is pure, it manifests spontaneously.
It is like the heavens opening a great treasury; when the heavens are clear and the earth is tranquil, the spirit reveals itself naturally.
In all cases, when wisdom and compassion unite with the Dao, the spirit acts without striving, yet its blessings and virtues cause the myriad things to respond.
Thus, it is clear that for the practitioner, wisdom unites with Heaven, and Heaven becomes pure;
compassion unites with Earth, which is gentle and harmonious, thereby nurturing all living beings. As the spirit remains eternally tranquil, blessings and virtues manifest of themselves.
Therefore, the Earth Deity pressed the earth with her toe, and immediately a multitude of jewels surged forth.
Through wisdom, she ultimately fulfills compassion with effortless spontaneity; thus, her divine function nourishes and sustains all things everywhere.
Therefore, the responsive manifestations of various jewels resulting from the power of retributive merit between heaven and earth do not arise from karma produced by the conceptualization of desire.
Through the spontaneous application of non-active, non-conceptual wisdom and compassion, they fill the realm of sentient beings, and the response of merit manifests of its own accord.

The Sūtra states: "I recall that since the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I have constantly followed the Bodhisattva, reverently guarding him and observing all his mental activities. This means that at the very inception of generating the resolve for enlightenment, one relies upon another.
Furthermore, taking the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance as the Buddha Dīpaṃkara constitutes the beginning of the arousal of the bodhicitta.

Beyond eons as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru, there was an eon named Adorned and a world named Moon Banner, where the Buddha was named Wondrous Eye; all the delusions and obstructions from the time of one's own initial arousal of the mind until then constitute those "dusty" eons.
Attaining the Dharma that cools delusion and confusion is the Moon Banner;
the manifestation of sublime wisdom is the Buddha Wondrous Eye.
Sublime wisdom is formless, its essence like space; indestructible and containing all phenomena, it is called the "Treasury."
From the passage "Having received from me this Dharma-gate of the indestructible treasury of wisdom" onwards, there is the advancement through the attribution of virtues.

The preceding section clarifies the completion of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), wherein wisdom and compassion are perfected amidst birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). This is like the spiritual nourishment of heaven and earth that is inexhaustible; one need not fear its retribution, as it is ultimately manifested by the spirits of heaven and earth.

The nine night goddesses (*rātridevatā*) below and one *Gopā* girl represent the ten stages (*bhūmi*), which nurture great loving-kindness and great compassion, thereby shattering the long night of ignorance regarding birth and death; these are symbolized by the night goddesses, as will be explained in detail below.

The ten spiritual friends mentioned above clarify how one enters the ocean of birth and death without emerging or sinking, thereby accomplishing wisdom and compassion and bringing the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) to full perfection, much like the manifold virtues of the ocean.

If, within the ocean of birth and death, one gradually employs great wisdom and great compassion with effortless spontaneity, one shatters the darkness of the long night, pervades the ten directions, and provides shelter for all sentient beings, allowing the divine function of the spirit to operate freely.
The Universal Pervasion primarily governs worldly dharmas, such as the assembly of night deities and others within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
From here on, all follow the patterns of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) to reach fulfillment at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
